title: Temperature Driven Mineral Accumulation Triggers Irreversible Failure in a High Strength CANDAN System
description: This study investigated the long term behavior of the novel Complete Ammonium and Nitrate removal via Denitratation Anammox over Nitrite process treating high strength wastewater under progressive cooling and subsequent warming. Under high substrate conditions, the reactor achieved stable total nitrogen removal by forming a dual reactor architecture comprising wall attached biofilms and suspended granules, wherein denitratation and anammox were spatially segregated but functionally integrated, enabling efficient NO3 and NH4 removal under favorable conditions. However, low temperature exposure significantly impaired microbial activity, especially in granules, resulting in sharp declines in NH4 removal . In contrast, denitratation remained resilient due to selective enrichment of cold adapted denitrifiers in biofilms. Importantly, the system failed to recover functionality after temperature restoration to 25. This was attributed to decoupled microbial mineral growth dynamics, where temperature inhibited biomass recovery but had negligible effects on hydroxyapatite crystallization. The mineral content increased sharply, causing the MLVSS/MLSS ratio to drop from 78.13 to 40.00, and biofilms served as preferential nucleation sites for mineral deposition. The resulting imbalance drove irreversible microbial suppression and system collapse. These results demonstrate that mineral accumulation, rather than microbial cold sensitivity alone, drives irreversible failure under coupled high substrate and low temperature stress. This study reveals a critical failure mechanism for high strength CANDAN systems and highlights the need to regulate inorganic precipitation in low temperature operational regimes.
